title: MoRA: Missing Modality Low-Rank Adaptation for Visual Recognition
claim: Modality alignment matters for missing-modality robustness, so fine-tuning should preserve cross-modal relations while still allowing modality-specific adaptation.
layout: 3 panels: two bar charts on top, geometric schematic below spanning width
description: The top row has two grouped bar charts that share a y-axis, Performance (%). Each chart covers MM-IMDb and Food101, with blue, orange and green bars for Both, Image and Text inputs. In (a), with unaligned ViT-B/16 and BERT encoders, performance falls to 14.9/15.2 on MM-IMDb and 1.4/1.2 on Food101 when one modality is missing. In (b), with aligned CLIP ViT-B/16, the single-modality bars stay much higher, for example 77.2 and 85.6 on Food101. The bottom panel (c) is a cartoon on a purple Pre-Training background and a yellow Fine-Tuning background. A blue image node and a red text node are joined by a black line labeled Gap. In pre-training the nodes sit still. In fine-tuning, the first panel shows both nodes moving together in black, and the second shows each node moving separately in its own color. The eye goes first to the colored bars, then down to the cartoon.
caption: Motivation for MoRA. (a) Performance comparison on MM-IMDb and Food101 datasets using unaligned vision and text encoders. (b) Performance comparison using aligned CLIP ViT-B/16 encoder. (c) During pre-training, modalities are aligned in embedding space with a gap; during fine-tuning, modalities should maintain their relationship while allowing modality-specific adaptations.
abstract: Pre-trained vision language models have shown remarkable performance on visual recognition tasks, but they typically assume the availability of complete multimodal inputs during both training and inference. In real-world scenarios, however, modalities may be missing due to privacy constraints, collection difficulties, or resource limitations. While previous approaches have addressed this challenge using prompt learning techniques, they fail to capture the cross-modal relationships necessary for effective multimodal visual recognition and suffer from inevitable computational overhead. In this paper, we introduce MoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that explicitly models cross-modal interactions while maintaining modality-specific adaptations. MoRA introduces modality-common parameters between text and vision encoders, enabling bidirectional knowledge transfer. Additionally, combined with the modality-specific parameters, MoRA allows the backbone model to maintain inter-modality interaction and enable intra-modality flexibility. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that MoRA achieves an average performance improvement in missing-modality scenarios by 5.24% and uses only 25.90% of the inference time compared to the SOTA method while requiring only 0.11% of trainable parameters compared to full fine-tuning.
